Operation Selection. We define an operation as a semantically complete end-to-end task that exercises a coherent unit of functionality, may span multiple APIs, and yields a checkable output. Operations provide a suitable granularity for performance comparison: project-level measurements are too coarse to distinguish functional paths, whereas API-level measurements are too fine-grained to represent complete functional tasks. We select an operation if it (i) represents core functionality, (ii) exercises a distinct performance-relevant implementation path, and (iii) can be executed on both C and the c2rust translation with outputs checked for equivalence. Multiple operations from the same project are retained only when they exercise distinct implementations. For example, we include both compression and decompression in bzip2 because exercise distinct implementation paths, and XXH64, XXH3, and XXH32 in xxHash because they implement distinct hashing algorithms. Workload Inputs. For each benchmark operation, we prefer established corpora or upstream-provided inputs, such as the Silesia corpus [ 41 ] and the Native JSON Benchmark [ 42 ] . When suitable upstream inputs are unavailable, we generate inputs deterministically from fixed parameters so that the C implementation and its c2rust translation process identical data. For input-sensitive operations, we use multiple sizes or formats. For inverse operations, we generate the corresponding forward output once with the C reference and reuse it unchanged for both implementations. Overall, the workloads span upstream, generated, and derived inputs across multiple sizes and formats, while preserving identical inputs for each C–Rust comparison. The selected workloads achieve 73.0–100.0% coverage of reachable functions in each project. III-B Experimental Settings Build Configuration. We use c2rust 0.22.1 to translate the C project into the corresponding Rust. For all comparisons, we compile C with clang-17 (17.0.6) and all Rust with rustc 1.77.0-nightly (2024-01-15), both using LLVM 17.0.6. C uses -O3 -flto ; Rust uses opt-level=3 , fat LTO, one codegen unit, and panic=abort . Both sides target the native CPU with AVX-512 disabled to ensure ISA parity; binary inspection confirms that neither emits AVX-512 instructions. Execution Environment. Measurements run on an Intel Core i9-10980XE CPU with 18 physical cores. To reduce system noise, we pin each run to an isolated physical core. We use the performance governor with turbo boost disabled to stabilize frequency, and Intel Resource Director Technology to reduce memory-bandwidth interference. Measurement Protocol. For each operation, corresponding C and Rust drivers invoke the respective implementations on the same workload input, and we measure them in pairs to obtain stable and directly comparable runtime estimates. When a single execution is too short for reliable timing, we use a fixed number of in-process repetitions to reach a minimum measurement duration, with the same repetition count for C and Rust. After warm-up, we collect paired measurements while alternating the C–Rust execution order across pairs to reduce temporal drift and order effects. We assess stability using the coefficient of variation (CV) of the pairwise Rust-to-C runtime ratios and repeat any unstable batch. For accepted batches, we remove ratio outliers using Tukey’s 1.5 × 1.5\times IQR rule [ 43 ] and report median runtimes. A pilot study on representative workloads showed that runtime estimates stabilized with a minimum measurement duration of 500 ms, five warm-up rounds, and 30 measurement pairs; we therefore use these settings throughout, consider a batch unstable when CV exceeds 3%, and allow at most two retries. Evaluation Metrics. We measure runtime using end-to-end wall-clock time. Let t C t_{C} and t R t_{R} denote the median execution times of C and Rust for the same operation and input. Relative runtime overhead is 𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟ℎ𝑒𝑎𝑑 = ( t R − t C ) / t C \mathit{overhead}=(t_{R}-t_{C})/t_{C} , where positive and negative values indicate slowdowns and speedups, respectively. To explain runtime differences, we decompose T CPU T_{\mathrm{CPU}} into dynamic work and per-instruction cost using R inst = I R / I C R_{\mathrm{inst}}=I_{R}/I_{C} and R CPI = 𝐶𝑃𝐼 R / 𝐶𝑃𝐼 C R_{\mathrm{CPI}}=\mathit{CPI}_{R}/\mathit{CPI}_{C} , respectively. III-C Experimental Procedure RQ1: Performance Divergence. Using the settings in Section III-B , we compare C with its c2rust translation for each operation–input pair and compute runtime overhead. RQ2: Cost Decomposition. Separately from runtime measurement, we measure retired instructions and CPU cycles over three runs, using their medians to compute R inst R_{\mathrm{inst}} and R CPI R_{\mathrm{CPI}} . For operations with materially higher CPI ( R CPI ≥ 1.05 R_{\mathrm{CPI}}\geq 1.05 ), we further apply TMA to identify the microarchitectural sources and report the corresponding c2rust translation and C differences in cycles per instruction. RQ3: Performance Issue Patterns. To characterize recurring code-level performance issues, we focus on operations for which c2rust incurs more than 3% runtime overhead over C. For each operation, we use perf to rank project-owned functions by sampled-cycle share and select the hottest functions accounting for at least 80% of sampled cycles; subsequent analysis is restricted to these functions. We examine the selected functions using three complementary evidence sources: whole-program optimized IR, compiler optimization remarks, and translated Rust source. Optimized IR. We compare whole-program optimized IR of C and its c2rust translation. We identify sites where translated Rust retains cost-bearing operations absent from C, such as bounds-check failure paths or saturating conversions. We also consider optimizer-relevant information in C but missing from Rust when its absence is accompanied by additional memory operations; Optimization Remarks. We compare source-mapped optimization remarks for C and its c2rust translation. We retain cases where LLVM applies a transformation to C but reports a blocking condition for the corresponding translated Rust code, and discard cases where the reported difference does not persist in the optimized IR; Translated Rust Source. We use The Rust Performance Book [ 44 ] as an inspection guide rather than a predefined taxonomy of performance issues. We derive concrete inspection criteria from relevant recommendations and apply them to hot translated Rust code. For example, guidance on heap allocation motivates inspection of repeated allocation and non-amortized buffer growth. We also examine recurring structures such as loop-invariant dispatch, pointer–length memory operations, raw-pointer traversal, and element-wise processing. We analyze the evidence in three steps. First, we record each performance-relevant candidate instance with its source region in the translated Rust, its manifestation in IR, compiler remarks, or source code, and its cost mechanism. Evidence from multiple representations referring to the same source construct and mechanism is merged. We then discard candidates whose code is not exercised by the workload (58) or belongs to the benchmark harness rather than the project (14), whose evidence does not support the stated mechanism (48), or whose C–Rust difference disappears in optimized IR (15). Of 404 candidates, 269 are retained as instances . Second, we group instances that share an underlying performance mechanism and admit a common remediation strategy. We retain only groups supported by at least three instances; each retained group defines a Performance Issue . This yields nine issues covering 268 of the 269 instances. The remaining instance concerns a state variable introduced by c2rust to emulate goto ; observed in only one function, it falls below the support threshold. Third, for each retained issue, we abstract its recurring manifestations into an Observed Pattern and derive an Optimization Direction targeting the underlying mechanism. For issues identified through IR or compiler remarks, we use paired C–Rust evidence to determine how to eliminate extra work absent from C or restore optimizations realized in C. For source-level issues, we map the underlying mechanism to a recommendation in The Rust Performance Book [ 44 ] , such as reusing a buffer across calls rather than allocating and freeing it on every call. An internal buffer is repeatedly allocated and freed, or grows by fixed increments through realloc . Typed values use memcpy / memset or hand-written byte-order helpers; known string lengths are recomputed with strlen . A loop processes adjacent elements individually ( e.g., out[i] = f(in[i]) ), or individually updates or compares elements. A loop accesses buffers through raw pointers ( e.g., ptr.add(i) ), with separately tracked bounds and implicit aliasing relationships. Table IV reports the nine recurring performance issues identified by our analysis, organized by their primary manifestation: residual runtime work (two), missed compiler transformations (two), and source-level performance issues (five). These categories are not mutually exclusive, as residual operations or retained calls may also inhibit downstream compiler transformations. Residual Runtime Work. Optimized IR reveals two recurring forms of residual work in translated Rust: Residual Bounds Checks and Redundant Conversion Saturation . Residual Bounds Checks persist despite provably valid access ranges. In BZ2_decompress , a nested traversal writes (*s).inUse[(i * 16 + j) as usize] , where i < 16 and j < 16 guarantee an index below 256. Yet the Rust IR retains a comparison against 256 and a branch to panic_bounds_check , while the corresponding C IR has no such failure path. The translated state-machine control flow prevents LLVM from recovering this range invariant. Expressing the traversal over a bounded slice makes the valid extent explicit and enables the redundant check to be eliminated. Redundant Conversion Saturation persists when operand ranges rule out saturation but the Rust IR retains saturating float-to-integer conversions. In heman , seven such conversions originate from fastFloor after inlining into heman_internal_generate_island_noise . The Rust IR uses llvm.fptosi.sat or llvm.fptoui.sat , whereas the corresponding C IR uses direct fptosi or fptoui . The operands are finite grid coordinates whose truncated values remain within the target integer range. Once these conditions are established, to_int_unchecked eliminates the redundant saturation. Missed Compiler Transformations. Paired C–Rust compiler remarks reveal two recurring missed transformations in translated Rust: Missed Loop Vectorization and Missed Hot-Callee Inlining . The Missed Loop Vectorization issue occurs when LLVM vectorizes a C loop but leaves its translated Rust counterpart scalar. In bzip2 , five hot decode loops exhibit this divergence. In a representative move-to-front loop that shifts mtfa entries, each array access carries a bounds check that adds a loop exit, and LLVM reports that it could not determine the number of loop iterations. Expressing the shift as a bounded slice operation can remove these checks and enable vectorization. The Missed Hot-Callee Inlining issue occurs when a hot call inlined in C remains uninlined in translated Rust because of missing inlining attributes or excessive estimated callee cost. In xxHash , the C implementation forces XXH3_accumulate_512_scalar to inline, whereas its translated Rust counterpart lacks the corresponding annotation and retains the call inside the hot stripe-processing loop. Restoring the missing inlining annotation can eliminate this barrier. Recurring Source-Level Patterns. Source inspection identifies five patterns in translated Rust code: Repeated Invariant Dispatch , Inefficient Buffer Management , Byte-Oriented Memory Operations , Scalar Element-Wise Processing , and Obscured Memory Access Properties . Unlike residual runtime work and missed compiler transformations, these patterns are characterized primarily by recurring source structures and their associated cost mechanisms. For example, Inefficient Buffer Management occurs in libzahl , where zmul_ll creates and releases four temporary integers at every recursion level, resizing their storage through libzahl_realloc when needed. Reusing preallocated scratch storage across recursive calls avoids this repeated allocation and resizing overhead. The Obscured Memory Access Properties issue arises when raw-pointer accesses leave bounds and aliasing relationships implicit, limiting LLVM’s ability to eliminate redundant loads. In libzahl , zrsh traverses limb arrays through raw-pointer accesses such as *ptr.offset(i) . The optimized Rust IR contains 73 static load instructions, compared with 24 in C, and lacks the !tbaa metadata present in the C IR. Consistently, GVN emits 46 missed-optimization remarks for Rust, versus 16 for C, frequently citing potentially aliasing writes as barriers to load elimination. Together, these observations suggest that obscured access relationships lead to conservative memory-dependence assumptions that inhibit load reuse. Recovering valid &[T] / &mut [T] views can expose these properties to LLVM and enable load elimination. Finding 3: We identify nine recurring performance issues in translated Rust, spanning residual work, missed compiler transformations, and source-level patterns, with optimization directions. V Approach Fig. 1: Workflow of PerfR The performance issues derived in § IV-C provide reusable guidance for recovering translation-induced performance loss. Applying this guidance to a new project requires localizing performance-critical code and identifying applicable rules. We therefore present PerfR , a rule-guided framework for recovering performance lost during C-to-Rust migration. Starting from a C project, PerfR obtains RawRust with c2rust , synthesizes workloads, and performs pre-optimization normalization (Figure 1 ). PerfR then localizes hot functions, identifies applicable optimization rules, and uses project context to guide precondition-aware LLM rewrites. Each rewrite is accepted only if it preserves functionality and improves performance. V-A Workload Synthesis Project-level optimization requires executable workloads to locate runtime hotspots and evaluate candidate rewrites. To capture end-to-end behavior and cost, PerfR organizes these workloads around operations that compose related APIs into complete tasks with checkable outputs. Starting from RawRust , PerfR synthesizes executable operations and harnesses and refines them using coverage feedback. This shared execution basis supports two complementary workload types: functional workloads provide diverse inputs for regression testing, while performance workloads provide sufficiently long executions for hotspot localization and performance validation. These internal workloads are independent of the benchmark workloads used for final evaluation. Operation and Harness Synthesis. PerfR first extracts the public API of RawRust , including pub functions and structs together with their module paths, and provides this information to the LLM. The LLM plans a bounded set of end-to-end operations, each representing a distinct functional task and identifying the API elements needed to realize it. Planning prioritizes core functionality and broad public-function coverage across the operation set. The planned operations, however, are not directly executable. For each operation, the LLM uses the associated API signatures to generate an executable harness and a small set of distinct seed inputs. The harness invokes the relevant APIs for each seed and produces an observable output. PerfR compiles and repeatedly executes the harness to check successful execution and output determinism. It also checks for output variation across distinct seeds to reject degenerate harnesses that ignore their inputs. When a check fails, the corresponding diagnostic feedback is returned to the LLM for revision [ 13 , 45 ] . This process continues within a fixed repair budget, and an operation is retained only when its harness passes all checks. Executability alone, however, does not ensure broad coverage of the public API. PerfR therefore measures public-function coverage across the retained operations using an instrumented build and their seed inputs. If coverage remains below the target, the uncovered functions and their signatures are provided to the LLM, which extends existing operations or introduces new ones. The harnesses and seed inputs are then generated and validated through the same process before coverage is recomputed. This feedback loop continues until the coverage target is reached or the refinement budget is exhausted, yielding the final operation set and validated harnesses. Functional Workload Synthesis. The validated harnesses establish operation executability, but their small seed sets provide limited behavioral diversity for regression testing. PerfR therefore fuzzes the seeds of each retained operation to generate a broader input corpus. Each generated input is executed repeatedly on the initial RawRust . Inputs that fail or produce nondeterministic outputs are discarded, while stable output digests are recorded as regression references.
